title: The services page a creative studio actually needs
metaTitle: Creative studio services page, in plain words
excerpt: List each service in the buyer's language, with an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. A grid of vague capabilities does not help a client choose.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table, a grid that only helps when each icon is a job someone can hire.
caption: A phone full of app icons on a pale table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is a service, as opposed to a capability?
faqs.answer: A service has an outcome, a boundary, and a next step a buyer can take. Motion, illustration, or a content model is a capability until someone can hire it alone and you can say what done means. If you cannot scope it from pages or screens, it is not ready to be a card.

faqs.question: How should services be ordered?
faqs.answer: Lead with the job most serious buyers need, the same kind of work the homepage just proved. Three to five services is enough. Use the same names in the navigation, the proposal, and the invoice.

faqs.question: What should the buyer bring in order to start?
faqs.answer: The current site, what is working, what must not break, and the date that is real. They do not need a finished agency brief. The page should say that, and the button should start a project rather than open a long form.

markdown:
A creative studio services page should list the work in the buyer's language. For a client who has already seen fifty portfolios, each service needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, which is to start a project.

A grid of vague capabilities does not help. "Brand, digital, campaign, innovation" is a floor plan of the studio, not a map the buyer can use. They came to see whether you do the job they have.

## Write the job, not the department

Start from the sentences a client actually says. "We need a site that explains the product." "We need the store moved without breaking checkout." "We need a small brand system the team will use." "We need the interface and the front end from the same people." Those sentences are your services. The internal names can stay in a planning doc.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a useful test. A page should help a person complete a task, and it should be clear who it is for. A services page is a choosing task. If a stranger cannot tell which block matches their job, the page was written for the studio's org chart.

Use words they already use. Site. Brand system. Store. Product interface. Ongoing partnership. Avoid "solutions," "offerings," and "360." A client who has sat through fifty portfolios has a reflex against those words. The reflex is fair. Those words have no boundary.

One service per job. Do not split "website design" and "website development" into two cards if you sell them as one engagement and the split only creates a second meeting. Do not merge "a logo" and "a full store migration" into one card because both are "creative." The buyer needs to see the edge.

## Outcome, boundary, next step

Each block on the page can be three short parts. Outcome: what is true when the work is done. Boundary: what this service does not include. Next step: how to start a project, and what to bring.

Outcome is a state, not a compliment. "A marketing site a stranger can understand in the first screen, with the repository in your account" is an outcome. "Award-winning digital craft" is a compliment. Compliments do not help a buyer compare you with the last studio they met.

Boundary is the part studios skip because it feels like a loss of work. It is the part that makes the outcome believable. A brand system engagement might not include a full website. A website engagement might not include a new name. A store migration might not include a new product line. Write the limit in the same block as the promise. The client who has been burned before is reading for it.

Next step should be the same action across the page, with a specific thing to bring. Start a project. Bring the current site, the page list, or the product job that is unclear. Do not give each service a different verb. "Discover," "transform," and "ignite" are not steps. They are decorations on the same button.

A block that cannot fill those three parts is not ready to be a service. It is a capability you sometimes use inside a service. Motion, illustration, and a content model belong inside the block they serve, unless you truly sell them alone and can name the outcome.

## Why a capability grid fails

A grid fails when every cell is a noun and none of them can be hired. Strategy. Identity. Experience. Engineering. Content. The buyer nods, because none of the words are wrong, and then they cannot remember what to ask for. The page felt complete and did nothing.

It also fails when the cells are written to rank for neighboring phrases. A services page that repeats "creative studio" in every heading is a brochure for a search engine. The client can tell. Say the job once, clearly, in the first lines, and then talk like a person.

Look at a cell and ask what you would put in a proposal the next day. If the answer is "it depends what they mean by innovation," the cell is not a service. Fold it into a service you can scope. Scoping is a list of pages or screens, a list of states, and the decisions that would change the date. A services page that cannot point at that kind of list will not survive a kickoff.

Public projects are a check on the grid. Down the Cove is a store migration and redesign, not a vague "ecommerce excellence" cell. Thomas Bewick is an editorial heritage site, not "content experiences." Wabisabi and Ballarat Box Sports are brand and site work with a visible point of view. If your services cannot caption a real project, they are still adjectives.

## Order the list the way they buy

Put the service most of your serious buyers need first. For many studios that is a marketing site or a product interface, not a renaming exercise. Lead with the job that matches the work on the homepage. If the homepage showed a store decision and the services page opens with "personal branding," the two pages are different studios.

Three to five services is enough. More than that and the buyer has to build their own package. Fewer than that is fine if it is true. A studio that designs and builds company sites does not need eight cards to look substantial. Substance is the boundary on the cards you do have.

Give each service a stable name you will use in proposals, in navigation, and on the invoice. If the navigation says "Sites" and the services page says "Digital flagship experiences," pick one. The buyer should not translate.

Under the list, one short paragraph can say how services combine. A brand system and a site are often one project. A site and a monthly partnership are often a sequence. Say the sequence. Do not make them add it up from icons.

## One service, written out

Here is a shape you can copy and then replace with your own limits.

Marketing sites. Outcome: a small set of pages that explain the offer and give one way to talk to you, built so you can edit the words and own the code. Boundary: not a product rebuild, not a photoshoot, not a month of campaign assets. Next step: start a project with the current URL and the list of pages you think you need.

Read it aloud. If you stumble on a noun, the noun is wrong. If the boundary is empty, you will argue about it later in the comments. If the next step is "hop on a call to jam," you have not decided what the buyer should bring.

Do the same for the other services you truly sell. Product interfaces, for a team that has outgrown a template and needs fewer screens. Brand systems small enough that engineers will open them. Store work where the migration plan is part of the design. Partnerships for the month after launch, when the real sentences arrive.

Hanabi's own work sits in that kind of list: interface design, production front ends, brand systems, ecommerce, and small automations when they are actually in scope. The point is not to copy the list. The point is that each line can be hired.

## The page around the list

The list is the body. The top of the page still has a job. Two short paragraphs should say who the services are for and what the buyer will be able to do when they finish reading. They should not preview every card in vaguer words. If the opening repeats the cards, cut the opening.

Give the page a title a stranger can use. "Services" alone is a label inside your nav. A title that names the studio and the kind of client is easier to tell apart from the fifty other tabs they have open. Keep it factual. Do not stack every service name into the title in the hope that all of them will rank. One page, one purpose.

Say how an engagement is chosen, in one sentence under the list. Most buyers need one service. Some need a sequence, such as a brand system and then the site that uses it. Almost none need every card at once. That sentence keeps a nervous founder from asking for the whole menu because they are afraid of leaving something out.

Add a practical note about what you need in order to scope. The current URL. What is working. What must not break. The date that is real, as opposed to the date that was wished for. You are not collecting a ten-field form on this page. You are telling them the difference between a service they can buy and a wish that still needs a conversation.

Read the finished page next to the homepage. The decision on the homepage should be hireable as one of these services. If the homepage promises a kind of judgment the services page never names, one of the two pages is fiction. Fix the list, or change the homepage. Do not hope the buyer will reconcile them.

## After the list

The services page should end by pointing at proof, not at another grid. One project per service, with the decision in the caption. If you have no project for a service, do not advertise the service yet. A card without proof is a wish.

When you want a second pair of eyes on whether the list matches the work, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the services you have now, including the ones you suspect are only adjectives. The call should decide which jobs are real, which are capabilities inside a job, and what the next step on the page ought to say.

The page that has to carry the people, not the menu, comes after this one. A services list can be clear and still feel unstaffed. The [about page for a creative studio](/blog/how-a-creative-studio-should-write-an-about-page) is where you name who does the work and why this buyer should care. Write it after the services are in the buyer's language, so the people are attached to jobs, not to a founding myth.
